title: The actor's longing
hookLine: Talaputa, an actor turned monk, talks to his own restless mind (Theragatha, Talaputa)

lines: HE TALKS TO HIS OWN MIND.
cards: When. It's a word for waiting rooms, long drives, the last hour before the weekend. In one of the long songs in the brothers' book, an actor says it to himself over and over.

Talaputa led a troupe of players. In a sutta, he asks the Buddha what becomes of actors who make crowds laugh with truth and lies. The Buddha would rather not answer, then does, and Talaputa weeps, and asks to go forth.
In his song, he talks to his own mind.

teach.b: First, the longing. His song opens with a run of questions. When will I live alone in mountain caves?
When will I wear the rag robe and want nothing? When will I see clearly that it all passes? The Pali word is kada, and it comes back so often it becomes the poem's rhythm.

teach.h: HE SPEAKS TO THE MIND DIRECTLY.
teach.b: Further on, the questions stop, and he speaks to the mind directly, as if it were someone sitting across from him. You're the one who urged me into this life, he says, and now you pull the other way. Third, the tone.
It isn't only scolding. He reasons with the mind. He coaxes it.
He reminds it of the forest, the rain, the calling birds, the quiet it said it wanted.
Some readers hear an actor's craft in it: one man playing two parts on one stage, the restless mind and the patient monk, trading lines. Fourth, the ordinary day.
Talaputa doesn't pretend the restless mind belongs to someone else.

He also doesn't simply do what it says. He talks to it like someone he has to live with, and his song doesn't pretend one talking-to settles it. Verse after verse, the longing stays honest, and the conversation goes on.
Perhaps that's what an actor brought to the forest: the knack of hearing your own voice as one voice among several, and answering it.

how: Meditation teachers in several Buddhist traditions encourage students to meet a wandering mind with patience rather than harshness, and some point to Talaputa's song as an early example of speaking to one's own mind.

o: where, as in where should I go?
when, as in when will it be?
how long, as in counting days

s: Talaputa's song is spoken to the Buddha all the way through
for much of it he speaks to his own mind, as if it sat across from him.
before he became a monk, Talaputa led a troupe of actors
in a sutta he asks the Buddha about actors, weeps at the answer, and asks to go forth.
in his song he only scolds the mind
he also reasons with it and coaxes it.

games.q: you're Talaputa, a monk now, and your mind keeps pulling back toward the old life. what do you do?
o: speak to the mind directly: scold it, reason with it, coax it.
games.why: his song turns into a conversation with his own mind, part scolding, part coaxing. he doesn't deny it, and he doesn't simply obey it.

practice: Sit, and let the mind do what it does; when it wanders, and it will, speak to it the way you'd speak to a restless friend in the passenger seat: there you are, come back now.
Talaputa scolded and coaxed, so try only the coaxing, and notice whether a kind voice brings the mind home faster than a hard one.

wordCard.voice: Kada. When: the word Talaputa the actor-turned-monk asks again and again, speaking to his own restless mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: kada, when. Talaputa's question, asked over and over.

carryVoice: Your line: when will it be. Even a restless mind can be talked to kindly. Day eight hundred two, done.
